opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really important point to clarify, because "token" gets used in a few different ways and it can get confusing. In the context of ByT5 and Mr. T5, when I say "token," I'm really talking about the individual units that the model operates over, and in a byte-level model those are just bytes. So instead of having a subword tokenizer like BPE or SentencePiece that chunks text into pieces like "un," "believ," "able," ByT5 takes the raw UTF-8 byte sequence of the text and treats each byte as its own token. For English, that's roughly one token per character, and for many other scripts a single character might actually be two, three, or four bytes, so you get even more tokens.

That's sort of the core tradeoff. Byte-level modeling is really nice because you get rid of the tokenizer entirely: there's no fixed vocabulary, no out-of-vocabulary issues, it's more robust to spelling variations and noise, and it's more equitable across languages. But the sequences get much longer, and since attention scales with sequence length, that makes byte-level models a lot more expensive to train and run.

So with Mr. T5, which stands for MergeT5, when I talk about tokens I'm still referring to those byte-level units at the input. The idea is that the model learns to dynamically delete or merge some of those byte tokens partway through the encoder, after a few layers have already had a chance to contextualize the information. So the "tokens" in the later layers are a reduced set of the original byte representations, and the model decides which ones to keep based on what it's learned. The point is that you keep the flexibility of operating on raw bytes but recover much of the efficiency you'd get from a shorter, subword-like sequence, without hard-coding a tokenizer up front.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says that in ByT5 and Mr. T5, tokens are the byte-level units the model operates on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I try to be careful about, because "token" gets overloaded a lot in this space. When I say "token" in the context of ByT5 and MrT5, I'm really just using it to mean the basic unit of the input sequence that the model is operating on, whatever that happens to be. So for a standard model like T5, a token is a subword, something produced by a tokenizer like SentencePiece, where you might have a whole word or a chunk of a word as a single unit. For ByT5, there's no subword tokenizer at all. The model takes in raw UTF-8 bytes, so each byte is its own position in the sequence. In that setting, I'll still say "token," but I mean a byte, and I'll usually say "byte" explicitly to avoid confusion.

The reason this matters so much for MrT5 is that the whole motivation for the work is sequence length. If you encode text as bytes instead of subwords, your sequences get roughly four to five times longer for English, and much longer for languages that don't fit as compactly in UTF-8. That blows up your compute, because attention scales with sequence length. So MrT5 is essentially about learning to delete bytes from the sequence partway through the encoder, so that the later layers of the model operate on a much shorter sequence. When I talk about "deleting tokens" in MrT5, I mean deleting positions in that byte-level sequence, and the model is learning a soft gating mechanism to figure out which bytes are not carrying much information and can be dropped.

So the short version is: "token" for me is the unit the model sees. For ByT5 and MrT5 that's a byte, and the interesting part is that MrT5 ends up implicitly learning something that looks a little like tokenization, because the bytes it keeps tend to merge information from the bytes it deleted. But it's doing that end to end, inside the model, rather than with a fixed, hand-designed vocabulary up front.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says that for ByT5 and MrT5, a token means a byte—the unit at each position in the model’s input sequence.

Mr. T5 starts with that same byte sequence, and its deletion mechanism removes some of those positions from the sequence the remaining encoder layers process.

sol-6.1.text: I’m using “token” to mean an element in the sequence the model processes, rather than necessarily a word or a subword. In ByT5, those input elements are bytes, so a single word spans multiple tokens. Mr. T5 starts with the same byte-level input, but learns to shorten that sequence inside the encoder by dropping some of those positions. So when I say “token,” the distinction is whether I mean an input byte or a position in that shortened internal sequence.
